title: Caccetta-Häggkvist Conjecture (Conjecture 1.1)
statement_text: For every integer $k \geq 1$, and all $n > 0$, every $n$-vertex digraph in which every vertex has out-degree at least $n/k$ has girth at most $k$.
context_text: One of the most well-known open questions in graph theory, especially for $k = 3$, with numerous partial results. The paper studies a bipartite analogue and shows that this conjecture implies the bipartite version (Conjecture 1.2).
paper_contribution: Shows that the Caccetta-Häggkvist conjecture implies the bipartite analogue Conjecture 1.2; uses CH-approximations to prove 1.2 for $k = 1, 2, 3, 4, 6$, and all $k \geq 224{,}539$.
paper_title: Short directed cycles in bipartite digraphs

title: Conjecture 1.2
statement_text: For every integer $k \geq 1$, if $G$ is a bipartite digraph, with $n > 0$ vertices in each part, and every vertex has out-degree more than $n/(k+1)$, then $G$ has girth at most $2k$.
context_text: Digraphs are finite without loops or parallel edges, but may have both $uv$ and $vu$ (directed 2-cycles). A digraph has girth at most $k$ if it has a directed cycle of length at most $k$; it is bipartite if its underlying graph is, and a bipartition of it is one of the underlying graph. The Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture states that every $n$-vertex digraph with all out-degrees at least $n/k$ has girth at most $k$; it is open for every $k\ge3$. This bipartite analogue is motivated by the following example: take disjoint sets $V_1,\dots,V_{2k+2}$ of size $t$ and make every vertex of $V_i$ adjacent from every vertex of $V_{i-1}$ (indices mod $2k+2$); this gives a bipartite digraph with parts of size $n=(k+1)t$, all out-degrees exactly $n/(k+1)$, and no directed cycle of length at most $2k$. The authors show the conjecture is implied by the Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture, and, using good approximate versions of Caccetta–Häggkvist, prove it for $k=1,2,3,4,6$ and all $k\ge224{,}539$. They also prove it when every vertex has in-degree and out-degree exactly $\alpha n$ with $\alpha>1/(k+1)$.
paper_title: Short directed cycles in bipartite digraphs

title: Conjecture 1.5
statement_text: For every integer $k \geq 1$, and every pair of reals $\alpha, \beta > 0$ with $k\alpha + \beta > 1$, if $G$ is a non-null bipartite digraph with bipartition $(A, B)$, where every vertex in $A$ has out-degree at least $\beta|B|$, and every vertex in $B$ has out-degree at least $\alpha|A|$, then $G$ has girth at most $2k$.
context_text: Digraphs are finite without loops or parallel edges, but may have both $uv$ and $vu$ (directed 2-cycles). A digraph has girth at most $k$ if it has a directed cycle of length at most $k$; it is bipartite if its underlying graph is, and a bipartition of it is one of the underlying graph. The Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture states that every $n$-vertex digraph with all out-degrees at least $n/k$ has girth at most $k$; it is open for every $k\ge3$. For $\alpha=\beta$ this conjecture is equivalent to the authors' bipartite analogue of Caccetta–Häggkvist (a bipartite digraph with $n>0$ vertices in each part and all out-degrees more than $n/(k+1)$ has girth at most $2k$), which they prove for $k=1,2,3,4,6$ and $k\ge224{,}539$; letting $\beta\to0$ it implies the Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture, so it would be optimistic to hope to prove it for $k=3$. For each $k$, if true it is best possible for infinitely many pairs $(\alpha,\beta)$, via circulant-type constructions. It is easy for $k=1$, and the authors prove it for $k=2$ (if $2\alpha+\beta>1$ the girth is at most four), which is their fundamental tool; for $k=3,4$ they prove the weakening where $k\alpha+\beta>1$ is replaced by $\alpha+\beta\ge2/(k+1)$.
